page: Amazon Web Services r7g.2xlarge is a memory-optimized server instance powered by custom AWS Graviton3 processors. Built on the 64-bit ARMv8 architecture with Neoverse-V1 cores, this instance provides 8 dedicated physical cores and 8 vCPUs with a single thread per core. It features a 2.6 GHz clock speed, 64 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache. The instance is equipped with 64.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high resource density of 8.0 GB of RAM per core. It operates on the AWS Nitro hypervisor, lacks local storage, and provides a baseline network bandwidth of 4 Gbps.

Benchmark data reveals strong memory performance, with a passmark memory score and read-only large-block memory bandwidth of 184.3 GB/sec both ranking in the top 25%. However, raw computational benchmarks present some tradeoffs. The passmark CPU score of 6073.06 and CPU encryption test of 1104.87 fall into the bottom 25%, reflecting weaker performance in cryptographic operations, which is also indicated by the lack of advanced vector and matrix extensions. Other processing metrics, such as stress-ng single-core and multi-core performance, fall within the average range.

Given the high memory-to-vCPU ratio and strong memory bandwidth, the r7g.2xlarge is designed for memory-intensive workloads. Passmark database operations average 8026.68, and Redis SET operations reach 13.53 million operations per second, indicating suitability for in-memory databases, caching layers, and data buffering. Conversely, poor performance in text generation for small LLM models and prompt processing for medium models suggests it is less suited for heavy machine learning inference. The ARM-based architecture offers qualitative cost efficiency by delivering high memory density and competitive memory throughput per resource unit compared to traditional x86 alternatives.

It features 64.0 GB of RAM, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core, and runs on the Nitro hypervisor with 4 Gbps baseline network bandwidth. Local storage is not included. Performance benchmarks highlight strong memory capabilities, with large-block read-only memory bandwidth reaching 184.3 GB/sec, placing it in the top 25%. However, CPU-bound cryptographic and raw processing tests show weaker results, with the Passmark CPU score falling in the bottom 25%. This profile makes the instance highly efficient for memory-bound applications, such as Redis caching and database operations, while presenting tradeoffs for compute-heavy or cryptographic workloads.
